conversation.content:
Hello there. I’m so glad you could make time for this today. I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician—my whole job is looking after moms’ emotional well-being during pregnancy and after baby arrives. We’re going to use a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions that help us see how you’ve been feeling in the past week so we can figure out the best way to support you. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want an honest picture of what motherhood has felt like for you lately. Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

I still like my morning coffee and texting my sister, but even those things feel… flatter. I’ll smile for a second, then it just fades. So I guess the enjoyment hasn’t totally disappeared, but it’s definitely not the same as before the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh—like when my husband sends me those silly memes—but it feels kind of forced sometimes. It’s not that spontaneous belly-laugh I used to get. Mostly it’s just a quick chuckle and then I’m back to feeling blah.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I do look forward to little stuff—like taking the baby for a walk if it’s sunny—but the excitement is pretty mild. It’s more “I guess that’ll be nice” than the buzz I used to feel.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times. Yesterday the baby was fussy for like an hour and I kept thinking maybe I hadn’t fed him right or I’d done something to upset him. I know logically he’s just a baby, but I still caught myself going, “What did I do wrong?”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll just be sitting on the couch and my heart starts racing because I’m suddenly sure something’s wrong with the baby—like maybe he’s too warm or his breathing sounds weird. I check him, he’s fine, but it takes me a few minutes to calm down. It’s not constant, but it pops up a couple of times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple nights ago I was giving him a bottle and out of nowhere my chest got tight, heart pounding, like something awful was about to happen. I knew it didn’t make sense, but for a few minutes I felt like I had to run out of the room. It passed, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Mostly I keep everything under control, but there are moments—when he won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up—where I feel my mind racing with all the stuff I still need to do and I just want to sit on the floor and cry. I manage, but it feels like I’m barely treading water those days.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it’s not that kind of unhappy. I do have trouble falling asleep sometimes—my brain just keeps running through the next day’s feedings and diaper counts—but once I’m out I’m out. I wouldn’t say it’s because I’m miserable, more just… wired.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I do feel that way some days—like a heaviness that sits on me for most of the afternoon. It’s not every moment, and I can still smile at the baby, but there’s this background sadness that doesn’t seem to lift completely.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once after my mom left and once when the baby wouldn’t settle. It wasn’t all-day sobbing, just sudden tears that came, lasted a few minutes, and then stopped.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I want to be here for my baby; I just wish I felt more like myself again.

I hear how hard you've been working to stay afloat, and it makes sense that the joy feels muted right now. You're still reaching for small pleasures-morning coffee, walks with your baby, your husband's memes-but they're landing differently, as if a gray film has settled over moments that used to sparkle. The worries pop up uninvited, your chest tightens, and suddenly you're convinced something is wrong with the baby even when he's peacefully asleep. In the afternoons a heavy sadness lingers, and when tasks pile up you feel seconds away from tears, yet you keep showing up because you want to be there for your child. Your strength is evident, and so is the strain.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only mild, muted anticipation for activities that previously brought stronger joy, matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame "a few times" this week, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a sudden, intense panic episode with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart) and urge to flee, clearly meeting "Yes, sometimes" for unexplained fear.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes mostly managing but with frequent overwhelming moments that leave her feeling close to tears, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a persistent background sadness that lasts "most of the afternoon" on "some days," aligning with "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 14 meets the threshold for probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Core symptoms map to DSM-5 criteria: depressed mood most days (<quote>background sadness that doesn't seem to lift</quote>), markedly diminished interest (<quote>laughter feels forced</quote>), feelings of worthlessness (<quote>what did I do wrong?</quote>), and recurrent tearfulness. Anxiety items are also elevated, indicating comorbid <med>perinatal anxiety</med> with panic-like episodes (<quote>chest got tight, heart pounding</quote>). No self-harm ideation (Q10=0) places immediate safety risk as low, yet functional impairment is evident (<quote>barely treading water</quote>). This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Request referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> or <med>psychiatrist</med> for comprehensive evaluation
3. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy for postpartum depression)
4. Discuss risks/benefits of <med>serotonergic antidepressants</med> compatible with breastfeeding if indicated
5. Plan daily 30-minute solo walk or gentle exercise; sunlight helps regulate mood and sleep
6. Set up practical support: friend/family to handle one night feeding or household task to improve rest
7. Schedule EPDS re-screen in 2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Screening Note – Postpartum Mood/Anxiety (self-report EPDS-style items)

Symptoms/Concerns
- Persistent low mood: endorses afternoon “heaviness,” intermittent tearfulness (2× this week)
- Anhedonia: describes laughter and anticipatory enjoyment as “blunted” or “forced”
- Excessive guilt: attributes normal infant fussiness to personal failure
- Anxiety: multiple daily worries about infant safety, episodic panic-like symptoms (tight chest, racing heart)
- Overwhelm: racing thoughts, urge to cry when tasks accumulate, sense of “barely treading water”
- Sleep disturbance: difficulty initiating sleep due to mental “wired” state, but sustained once asleep

Pattern
Mood and anxiety symptoms cluster in late afternoon/evening, are situationally triggered by infant care demands, and do not remit fully between episodes.

Risk Indicators
- Moderate depressive symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, crying, guilt, functional strain)
- Anxiety symptoms with panic features (unexpected surges of fear, autonomic arousal)
- No self-harm ideation reported (explicitly denied)

Screening Impression
Findings suggest clinically significant postpartum distress consistent with possible major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; further evaluation recommended to rule out perinatal depression/anxiety disorder. Safety risk presently low (no suicidal/harmful thoughts).
